Laden
lā'dn
v. and adj. (loaded; burdened; the archaic past participle of lade)
Old English hladan, to load. The Authorized Version uses the strong participle laden where modern English says loaded, and Scripture loads three very different things.

Biblical Definition

First, a load of kindness: Joseph “sent after this manner; ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt, and ten she asses laden with corn and bread and meat for his father by the way” (Gen 45:23), sent by a brother whom the brothers had sold. Then a load of provision on an errand: “Jesse took an ass laden with bread, and a bottle of wine, and a kid, and sent them by David his son unto Saul” (1Sa 16:20) — a shepherd boy carrying a hamper to the king he would replace. Then a load of guilt: “Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters” (Isa 1:4). And finally the invitation that answers the third: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28). The Greek there is a perfect passive participle — those who have been loaded, and are still carrying it — and the verse is addressed not to the notoriously wicked but to people bent under a religion of works, since the chapter's next line offers a yoke that is easy and a burden that is light. Christ does not offer to remove all burdens. He offers to exchange the load.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines laden as the participle passive of lade: loaded; charged with a burden or freight; oppressed.

LADEN, pp. of lade. Loaded; charged with a burden or freight.

LADE, v.t. To load; to put on or in, as a burden or freight.

Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden. Matt. xi.

Key Scripture

Gen 45:23 — "And to his father he sent after this manner; ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt, and ten she asses laden with corn and bread and meat for his father by the way."

Isa 1:4 — "Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward."

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Modern Corruption

Matthew 11:28 is read as a general offer of relief from a busy life, when its context makes it an offer of relief from a religion of works — and the rest promised is a yoke.

expand to see more

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden is quoted more often than almost any verse in the Gospels, and usually with a modern load in mind: overwork, exhaustion, an over-full calendar, the general strain of contemporary life. Christ's hearers were carrying something else. The chapter has just pronounced woe on the cities that saw His mighty works and did not repent, and thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent; the burden in view is the one Matthew 23:4 describes, laid on men's shoulders by the scribes and Pharisees — heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, which they themselves would not move with one of their fingers. That is a religion of merit, and it is the specific weight the invitation lifts. The proof is in what follows immediately, which is very rarely quoted with it: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. He does not promise an unyoked life. He promises a different yoke, worn with Him, from a Master who is meek and lowly — and the rest offered is rest unto the soul, which is what a man loaded with iniquity most needs and least expects to be given for nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nasa' (H5375), to lift, to bear, to carry; kabed (H3513), to be heavy, weighty; Greek phortizo (G5412), to load, to burden.

expand to see more

Hebrew nasa' (H5375) — to lift up, bear, carry away; used both of bearing a load and of bearing away sin; Genesis 45:23, Isaiah 53:12.

Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to be heavy, weighty, burdensome; the same root as kabod, glory, which is weight; Isaiah 1:4, Exodus 5:9.

Greek phortizo (G5412) — to load, to burden; the heavy laden whom Christ calls, and the burdens the lawyers laid on men; Matthew 11:28, Luke 11:46.

Usage

"“Ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt” — a load of kindness from a sold brother."

"“A people laden with iniquity” — the load Isaiah names."

"“All ye that labour and are heavy laden” — and the yoke offered in exchange."
